transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Yeah, um… I guess I’m here because I feel like I’m always running hot. Like there’s this motor in me that just doesn’t shut off, even when I’m supposed to be calm or waiting around.

And lately it’s been… causing problems at the firehouse. Which is frustrating, because I love the job. I mean, it’s not like sitting at a desk all day—my brother tried that insurance thing for a while and I don’t know how people do it—but even in a busy place like the station, I’m still too keyed up, I guess. It’s starting to get me in trouble.
Does this revved-up feeling come in distinct periods where you're noticeably more energized than usual?

Not really like… distinct periods, I don’t think. It’s more constant. Like I said, I feel like I’m always running hot, like there’s this motor that just doesn’t shut off.

I mean, at the firehouse there’s already noise and movement and calls and guys messing around in the kitchen, so sometimes it blends in, you know? But lately it’s been getting me in trouble there because even when things are supposed to be calm, I still feel revved up.
Do you often have trouble staying focused on tasks or conversations, even when you're trying to pay attention?

Yeah, definitely. I mean, I try to pay attention, especially when it matters. Like in briefings at the station or when we’re doing drone training, I’ll be good for the first few minutes, like, “Okay, I’m locked in.”

Then I kind of snap back and realize I’ve just been staring at the map or the screen, and I didn’t actually catch half of what command was saying. And then I’m trying to piece it together from context, which is… not great. Especially because everyone else seems to just hear it once and move on.
When you think back to grade school, were you already the kind of kid who was restless or had trouble paying attention?

Yeah, apparently I was. I don’t remember all of it clearly, but my mom sure does. She says I was the kid who couldn’t stay in his seat, always blurting out answers before the teacher finished, losing homework even when I’d actually done it.

Which is funny because she always says I was smart enough to do the work, I just… didn’t get it turned in, or I’d get notes sent home. And then I’d be in trouble, and I’d swear I was gonna do better, and then same thing again.
Do you often blurt things out or act before thinking, even when you know it might cause problems?

Yeah. I mean, I don’t always mean to, but it happens a lot at the station. Like if the guys are talking through a plan and I already see what I think the answer is, I’ll just jump in with it.

And then halfway through I realize I cut somebody off, or I kind of threw off the flow of what they were explaining. It’s not like I’m trying to be a jerk, it’s just… the thought is already there and my mouth goes before I’ve checked myself. Then afterward I’m like, why didn’t I just wait two seconds?
Do you spend a lot of time worrying about different parts of your life, even when there isn’t a clear reason to?

I don’t know if I’d call it worrying, exactly. I mean, everybody’s got stuff on their mind, right? Bills, the house, work stuff, whether I forgot to get groceries—actually I did forget milk yesterday, which is annoying because my kid only likes that one kind—

Sorry. What was the question? Like worrying for no reason? I’m not sure. I don’t think I sit around worried all day, if that’s what you mean.
Do these focus and restlessness problems happen in other parts of your life too, like at home?

Yeah, definitely at home too. Like on my days off, I’ll think, okay, I’m gonna just sit with my wife and kid and watch a movie or play a quiet game or whatever, and I last maybe… I don’t know, not long.

I’ll start talking through the show, or I’ll get up because I remembered something in the garage, like I should check a tool or straighten something up real quick. Then I’m in there messing with that, and my wife’s like, “Are you coming back?” And I didn’t even mean to leave for that long.

Even just sitting at the table, I’m shifting around or getting up before everyone’s really done. It’s not that I don’t want to be with them. I do. I just have a hard time staying still and doing the quiet family stuff.
Did these problems get noticeably worse after a specific stressful event?

Not like one big bad event, no. It’s more… it got noticeably worse after the schedule changed at work. About a year and five months ago, when they added those longer rotating shifts, and then all the extra documentation stuff, plus the drone duties.

Which, I mean, the drones are interesting, don’t get me wrong—there’s a lot you can do with them on a scene—but it’s another thing to keep track of. So yeah, not one stressful event exactly, more that workload and shift change started around then, and that’s when it became a real problem.
Since the schedule changed, have you been getting less sleep?

I’m not really sure. I mean, the shifts are longer, so the whole day feels thrown off, but whether I’m actually sleeping less… I haven’t really tracked it.

Sometimes I get home and I’m still wound up, and then I end up doing little things around the house, like checking the doors or looking for something I left in my truck, and then suddenly it’s later than I thought. But I don’t know if that means less sleep exactly or just weird timing. I’d have to think about it.
When you feel revved up, does it feel like nervousness or fear?

Not really fear, no. I mean, I don’t feel scared exactly. It’s more like I’m just… running hot all the time, like the motor won’t shut off.

That’s kind of why I’m here, honestly. Lately it’s been getting me in trouble at the firehouse, because I’m always going, always keyed up, and then I—well, not nervous like something bad is about to happen, just revved. Like I can’t idle.
When you feel revved up, is it usually because your mind is stuck on worries you can’t turn off?

I don’t know if I’d call it worries exactly. Sometimes my head’s just… busy, like there’s a bunch of stuff bouncing around, and then I’ll remember something random I meant to do.

Like the other night I was thinking about whether I put something back in the right compartment on the truck, and then that made me think about the garage at home, because I’ve got this shelf I keep meaning to fix, and then I’m looking for a tool and—sorry, I’m kind of getting off track.

So, stuck on worries? I’m not sure. It doesn’t always feel like worrying. More like my brain won’t slow down.
Do you often find yourself worrying so much that it’s hard to stop?

I don’t know… I mean, I wouldn’t say I’m sitting there worrying all the time, exactly. Sometimes I’ll get stuck on something, but then it turns into a whole other thing, like I’ll start thinking about one thing I forgot to do and then I’m remembering something at work, and then I’m thinking about the garage or my truck or—yeah.

So I guess it’s hard for me to tell if that’s worry or just my head not shutting up. It doesn’t feel like I’m afraid, more like I can’t land on one thought long enough to finish it.
Do you often feel unable to control your worrying?

I’m not sure I’d put it that way. Like, “worrying” makes it sound like I’m sitting there thinking something terrible’s going to happen, and that’s not usually how it feels.

It’s more like once my head gets going, I have a hard time steering it. I’ll start on one thought and then I’m off onto something else, and then something else. Like I’ll be trying to answer a text and suddenly I’m thinking about whether I left something in the wrong place, and then—sorry, that’s not really your question.

So… unable to control worrying? I don’t know. Unable to control where my thoughts go sometimes, yeah, but I don’t know if I’d call it worrying.
Before the schedule change at work, were you already having these same focus and restlessness problems as an adult?

Not really the same, no. I mean, I’ve always had days where I’m scattered, everybody does, especially with this job, but it became a real problem about… a year and five months ago, I guess.

That was when the schedule changed—longer rotating shifts—and then all the extra paperwork got piled on, plus the drone stuff. I remember because we were trying to figure out where to store the drone batteries and chargers, and there was this whole thing about the cabinet—sorry.

But yeah, before that change, it wasn’t like this level. Since then it’s been much harder to manage.
Before the schedule changed at work, were these focus and restlessness problems already causing you trouble in other adult settings?

Before the schedule change? I mean… I don’t think it was costing me like it is now.

The big trouble’s been at the firehouse lately. Like, it’s gotten to where people don’t trust me the same way with keeping track of details, and that’s hard to say because in that job trust is everything. I got pulled into a performance and safety meeting, which felt awful. And I’d been hoping to move toward more of a leadership role, but now it feels like that’s kind of slipping away because the crew can’t count on me consistently.

Sorry, that’s more about work than other settings. Before the schedule change, I don’t remember it causing that kind of trouble elsewhere.
Since the work schedule changed, do your symptoms get noticeably better when you’re away from work for several days?

I don’t really know. I haven’t tracked it that closely, I guess.

Like if I’m off for a few days, sometimes I’m just catching up on sleep or trying to get stuff done at home, and then the days kind of disappear. I’ll think, “Okay, I’m going to reset,” and then suddenly it’s the night before I go back and I’m trying to remember where my uniform pieces are—sorry.

So… noticeably better? Maybe a little just because I’m not at the station, but I’m not sure I could say it clearly gets better.
Do these focus and restlessness problems mostly happen because of the changes at work?

Yeah… I mean, that’s how it feels. It really became a problem after the work changes, about a year and five months ago.

The longer rotating shifts, all the extra documentation, and then the drone responsibilities got added in, and since then it’s just been… harder to keep up. Before that, I don’t think it was at this level.
Did the changes at work feel traumatic to you?

Traumatic? I don’t know if I’d use that word. I mean, it’s been stressful and frustrating, and I’ve definitely felt kind of thrown off by it.

When I hear “traumatic,” I think of calls we go on or bad scenes, not a schedule change, you know? Although the way it messed with everything… I don’t know. It’s hard to separate. The firehouse has its own rhythm, and when that changes, it feels like your whole life changes with it. Even stuff like when I eat or when I see people or when I’m trying to get laundry done—sorry, that’s probably not what you’re asking.

So, no, I’m not sure I’d call the work changes traumatic. More like overwhelming, maybe.
Do you feel the work changes are what caused these problems to become a real issue for you?

Yeah, I think so. I mean, that’s when it went from being manageable to feeling like a real problem.

It’s been about a year and five months now, since they added the longer rotating shifts and all the extra documentation, and then the drone duties on top of it. Before that, I had my ways of getting through the job, you know? Like everybody has their routine at the station, and then suddenly the routine wasn’t really there anymore.

So… yeah, I’d say the work changes are what made it become a real issue.
If the work schedule and duty changes had never happened, do you think these problems would still be causing major trouble for you now?

I mean… maybe not “major” in the same way, no. The work changes definitely pushed it into the open.

But I don’t know, because now it’s costing me trust at the firehouse, and that’s the part that really bothers me. I got pulled into a performance and safety meeting, which was… yeah, that was rough. And you know how it is in a crew—well, maybe you don’t, but if people feel like they can’t count on you to track the details, that follows you around.

I was hoping to move toward a leadership spot eventually, and now it feels like that’s slipping away. So if the schedule stuff hadn’t happened, maybe I wouldn’t be in this exact mess, but the trouble now is real.

target_item.manifestation: This has started costing me trust at the firehouse; I was pulled into a performance and safety meeting, and now my shot at moving into leadership feels like it’s slipping because the crew can’t count on me to track the details consistently.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the focus and restlessness symptoms were causing trouble or impairment in adult settings, which most directly matches functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Before the schedule change? I mean… I don’t think it was costing me like it is now.

The big trouble’s been at the firehouse lately. Like, it’s gotten to where people don’t trust me the same way with keeping track of details, and that’s hard to say because in that job trust is everything. I got pulled into a performance and safety meeting, which felt awful. And I’d been hoping to move toward more of a leadership role, but now it feels like that’s kind of slipping away because the crew can’t count on me consistently.

Sorry, that’s more about work than other settings. Before the schedule change, I don’t remember it causing that kind of trouble elsewhere.

ADHD remains strongly supported by childhood onset of inattention/hyperactivity/impulsivity across settings. An adjustment/stressor-related condition remains possible because marked worsening and occupational impairment began after the work schedule/workload change.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the adult worsening is better explained by chronic ADHD traits or by a stress-related reaction tied to the work schedule change.
doctor.question: Since the work schedule changed, do your symptoms get noticeably better when you’re away from work for several days?

target_item.reason: The question asks whether symptoms improve when away from work for several days, which concerns situational variation/context rather than any specific listed ADHD symptom, duration, onset, or impairment item.

patient.answer:
I don’t really know. I haven’t tracked it that closely, I guess.

Like if I’m off for a few days, sometimes I’m just catching up on sleep or trying to get stuff done at home, and then the days kind of disappear. I’ll think, “Okay, I’m going to reset,” and then suddenly it’s the night before I go back and I’m trying to remember where my uniform pieces are—sorry.

So… noticeably better? Maybe a little just because I’m not at the station, but I’m not sure I could say it clearly gets better.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are specifically tied to the work-related stressor, which would support a stress-related disorder over ADHD.
doctor.question: Do these focus and restlessness problems mostly happen because of the changes at work?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: It’s been a real problem for about a year and five months, ever since the longer rotating shifts and extra documentation and drone duties got added.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the problems are tied to the work changes, and this item captures that they became a real problem about a year and five months ago after the longer rotating shifts and added duties.

patient.answer:
Yeah… I mean, that’s how it feels. It really became a problem after the work changes, about a year and five months ago.

The longer rotating shifts, all the extra documentation, and then the drone responsibilities got added in, and since then it’s just been… harder to keep up. Before that, I don’t think it was at this level.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are better explained by a stress-related reaction to the work change versus longstanding ADHD by testing for a clear trauma response to the schedule/workload change.
doctor.question: Did the changes at work feel traumatic to you?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the work changes felt traumatic, which is about trauma or stressor impact rather than any ADHD symptom or listed requirement in the profile.

patient.answer:
Traumatic? I don’t know if I’d use that word. I mean, it’s been stressful and frustrating, and I’ve definitely felt kind of thrown off by it.

When I hear “traumatic,” I think of calls we go on or bad scenes, not a schedule change, you know? Although the way it messed with everything… I don’t know. It’s hard to separate. The firehouse has its own rhythm, and when that changes, it feels like your whole life changes with it. Even stuff like when I eat or when I see people or when I’m trying to get laundry done—sorry, that’s probably not what you’re asking.

So, no, I’m not sure I’d call the work changes traumatic. More like overwhelming, maybe.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptoms are linked to a non-traumatic stressor, supporting an adjustment disorder rather than ADHD.
doctor.question: Do you feel the work changes are what caused these problems to become a real issue for you?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: It’s been a real problem for about a year and five months, ever since the longer rotating shifts and extra documentation and drone duties got added.
target_item.reason: The question is asking whether the work changes triggered when the problems became a real issue, which matches the duration profile noting the problems began about 1 year and 5 months ago after longer rotating shifts, extra documentation, and drone duties were added.

patient.answer:
Yeah, I think so. I mean, that’s when it went from being manageable to feeling like a real problem.

It’s been about a year and five months now, since they added the longer rotating shifts and all the extra documentation, and then the drone duties on top of it. Before that, I had my ways of getting through the job, you know? Like everybody has their routine at the station, and then suddenly the routine wasn’t really there anymore.

So… yeah, I’d say the work changes are what made it become a real issue.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the symptom worsening is linked to a stressor and thus better fits an unspecified stress-related disorder rather than longstanding ADHD.
doctor.question: If the work schedule and duty changes had never happened, do you think these problems would still be causing major trouble for you now?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: This has started costing me trust at the firehouse; I was pulled into a performance and safety meeting, and now my shot at moving into leadership feels like it’s slipping because the crew can’t count on me to track the details consistently.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the symptoms would still be causing major trouble or impairment even without the work schedule and duty changes.

patient.answer:
I mean… maybe not “major” in the same way, no. The work changes definitely pushed it into the open.

But I don’t know, because now it’s costing me trust at the firehouse, and that’s the part that really bothers me. I got pulled into a performance and safety meeting, which was… yeah, that was rough. And you know how it is in a crew—well, maybe you don’t, but if people feel like they can’t count on you to track the details, that follows you around.

I was hoping to move toward a leadership spot eventually, and now it feels like that’s slipping away. So if the schedule stuff hadn’t happened, maybe I wouldn’t be in this exact mess, but the trouble now is real.

inference.note: Ruled out F43.9: the work changes were stressful/overwhelming but not traumatic, and the symptoms are better explained by longstanding ADHD features (childhood onset of inattention/hyperactivity-impulsivity across settings) that became functionally impairing after increased work demands.
